$comment: Per-node details for the tech tree popups, keyed by node or moonshot ID. Fields: brief (1-2 sentences), github (https://github.com/... issue, project or repo), lead (name or handle), team (list). Briefs are drafts: review and edit freely. Leave github/lead empty until a project exists.

R-COM1.brief: The simplest starting point for talking to a vehicle: a ready-made radio pair. Nearly everything else in the tree needs some kind of link, so this is where comms begin.

R-COM2.brief: Adds encryption on top of a basic radio link so nobody else can read or hijack the traffic. It is the secure foundation for the TAK bridge, the mesh and sensor nodes.

R-COM3.brief: Wired links made from copper or fiber cable. They are hard to jam, carry lots of data, and enable tethered drones, ROVs and crawlers that can't rely on radio.

R-COM4.brief: Uses beams of light to send encrypted data between vehicles, even while they move. Its hard part is pointing and tracking the beam in flight.

R-SEC1.brief: Gives every device a unique identity and secret keys, and a safe way to pair it with the network. Without it, nothing in OASA can tell trusted devices from strangers.

R-SEC2.brief: Lets the network swap out old keys and kick out lost or stolen devices. This keeps a mesh safe over time, and it is needed before the first encrypted mesh.

R-PWR1.brief: Safe battery packs with a battery management system that watches charge, heat and health. Every vehicle and node needs power, so this is the base for the rest of the power branch.

R-PWR2.brief: Charging batteries from sunlight. It lets nodes, boats and aircraft run far longer without a human swapping batteries.

R-PWR3.brief: Harvesting energy from wind, including kites that fly in the wind. It supports remote nodes and longer-running systems where sun is not enough.

R-PWR4.brief: Sending electrical power along a cable to a vehicle, so it can stay aloft or underwater as long as the cable is connected. Pairs with data links in the same tether.

R-PWR5.brief: Sending power through the air to a vehicle in flight using a laser or microwaves. It could someday keep aircraft up without landing, and it needs strong safety engineering.

R-CTL1.brief: A human flies, drives or steers the vehicle by hand over a radio link. It is the first control mode and the safe fallback for later autonomy.

R-CTL2.brief: Vehicles follow a list of waypoints on their own, using flight controller software like PX4 or ArduPilot. This unlocks the reference drones, rovers and boats.

R-NAV1.brief: Using satellite signals (GPS and similar) to know where a vehicle is. Autonomous control, maps and timing all depend on it.

R-NAV2.brief: A correction method that sharpens satellite positioning to a much finer level. It lets docks, mapping and ground robots know exactly where they are.

R-NAV3.brief: Finding your way when satellite signals are blocked, using cameras and motion sensors. Needed for caves, tunnels and underwater missions.

R-TIME1.brief: A shared clock across all OASA devices. Matching timestamps let video, direction finding and sound sensors line up their data.

R-TIME2.brief: A backup way to tell time and position using the mesh itself when GPS fails or is blocked. It helps communities stay connected in bad situations.

X-1.brief: Getting a camera feed from a vehicle to a screen. Video feeds AI, mapping and GPS-free navigation.

T-MAP1.brief: Shows OASA vehicles on the TAK map (ATAK, Cursor-on-Target) with their position, battery and status. It connects OASA to tools responders already use.

T-MAP2.brief: Tap a spot on the TAK map and a vehicle goes there. It turns the map from a display into a control surface.

T-NET1.brief: A first encrypted mesh of three to five nodes that pass traffic for each other. It proves the network design that everything bigger grows from.

T-NET2.brief: Teaches the mesh to choose the best route for data and send urgent messages first. This keeps control and video usable when the network is busy.

T-NET3.brief: Lets control of a vehicle pass smoothly between ground stations and operators. It makes teams and long missions possible.

T-NET4.brief: Growing the encrypted mesh to 100 or more nodes without it falling over. This is the step toward a regional network that sustains itself.

T-NET5.brief: A secure gateway connecting OASA to Meshtastic and LoRa networks. It lets cheap, low-power radios and community networks share messages with OASA.

T-PAY1.brief: A common mechanical and electrical plug for payloads like cameras, sensors and arms. The aim is one payload design that fits many vehicles.

T-LOG1.brief: A flight-recorder style log format for every OASA device. Good logs help find failures, improve designs and prove what happened.

T-AI1.brief: A small computer module on the vehicle that runs AI, like spotting objects in video. It enables detection, inspection and smarter missions without a cloud connection.

T-AI2.brief: Type or say a goal such as "survey the north field, find hogs" and the system turns it into a mission plan. It makes fleets easier for non-experts to use.

T-AI3.brief: Steer a mission in the field by voice, with commands like "closer" or "go further north." It builds on sentence-based missions and the TAK map.

T-VID1.brief: Video that is sent only when someone asks for it, so it doesn't clog the mesh. It lets operators look through a vehicle's camera when it matters.

T-TSK1.brief: Vehicles report whether they are busy or idle, accept tasks, and hand them off to each other. This is the basis for fleets and teams.

T-TSK2.brief: A carrier vehicle launches a small scout, which flies out and returns with information about where to go next. A first step toward vehicles working as teams.

T-DOCK1.brief: A vehicle lands accurately on a dock using precise positioning and sensors. It is the first step toward missions that start and end with no human.

T-DOCK2.brief: A dock that charges vehicles by itself once they land. Combined with precision landing, it allows repeated missions without human help.

T-SIM1.brief: A software copy of vehicles and environments where designs and missions can be tested safely. It lets contributors work and train without hardware.

T-BENCH1.brief: Standard test rigs and software for checking that parts and builds work as promised. It keeps quality up as more chapters build the same designs.

T-RF1.brief: Scans the radio spectrum to see which signals are around. Helps find clear channels and spot interference.

T-RF2.brief: Using several antennas to find which direction a radio signal comes from, then drawing bearings on the TAK map. Useful for tracking down interference.

T-RF3.brief: Combining antennas to aim radio energy toward a target. It gives longer, stronger links and is needed for laser links and high-altitude platforms.

T-NODE1.brief: A portable, backpack-sized mesh node kit with radio, battery and encryption. Anyone can carry it to extend the network.

T-NODE2.brief: Weatherproof node kits for towers, vehicles and homes, with solar power. They give the mesh a fixed backbone and wider coverage.

A-1.brief: A low-cost quadcopter that everyone can build and fly. It is the main aircraft many branches build on, from inspection to rescue.

A-2.brief: A standard fixed-wing airplane design. Generally covers more distance on less power than quads, which suits surveys and long-range work.

A-3.brief: An aircraft that takes off like a quad and flies like a plane, combining both reference designs. It brings long range without needing a runway.

A-4.brief: A drone held up by a cable that supplies power, so it can hover for a long time. Useful as a high relay or camera point.

A-5.brief: A fixed-wing aircraft with solar panels that gain energy while flying. It is the step toward very long flights.

A-6.brief: A solar-powered glider designed to fly at high altitude for a long time. It could act as a relay or camera platform, a "poor man's satellite" for coverage.

A-7.brief: A drone that flies between others and the ground station to pass their radio traffic along. It extends the range of small drones.

A-8.brief: Aircraft that use rising air, ridge winds and wind gradients to stay up while saving energy, like birds do. Smart energy-aware control makes flights much longer.

A-9.brief: An ultralight solar aircraft built to stay aloft for long periods, using sun by day and stored energy and soaring by night. A design study toward an atmospheric satellite.

A-10.brief: A robot that flies by flapping wings, like a bird or insect, and builds on the reference quad. Aims at quiet wildlife monitoring.

L-1.brief: A kite that carries sensors or radios aloft using wind. It is the base for the solar kite, the kite generator and the tethered aerostat.

L-2.brief: A kite with lightweight solar panels that powers sensors up in the air. It gives a long-running overhead sensing point.

L-3.brief: A kite that makes electricity from wind high above the ground. Could power remote nodes and charging stations.

L-4.brief: A gas-filled balloon held by a cable, giving a stable high platform for radios and cameras. The cable can carry power and data.

L-5.brief: A solar-powered blimp that can steer and hold its position. It can stay over an area for long periods as a sensor or relay.

L-6.brief: A large blimp that lifts heavier sensors and mesh repeaters over an area. Meant for emergencies where ground networks are down.

L-7.brief: A large blimp that carries smaller drones, launching and recovering them in the air. It extends their reach and lets one platform run many missions.

G-1.brief: A basic ground robot on wheels or tracks. It is the main ground reference platform for hauling payloads, inspecting and exploring.

G-2.brief: A robot that walks on legs, so it can cross stairs and rough ground that wheels can't. Needs strong navigation, often built with ROS 2.

G-3.brief: A robot that spots and picks up litter in a city, using an arm and AI vision. It helps keep streets clean without constant human effort.

G-4.brief: A ground vehicle that carries drones and charges them. It moves the dock to where the work is.

G-5.brief: A robot that explores caves, tunnels and collapsed buildings and builds a 3D map on its own. It drops relay nodes as it goes to keep a link home.

G-6.brief: A robot that clears snow and ice from sidewalks first and later streets. It helps neighbors who can't easily clear their own paths.

G-7.brief: A robot that helps elderly and disabled neighbors by guiding them or delivering items. It needs to be safe and easy to use around people.

S-1.brief: A boat for surveying lakes, rivers and coasts. It is the base for water sampling, cleanup and carrier boats.

S-2.brief: A floating buoy that is a mesh node and weather station. It extends the network onto the water and reports local conditions.

S-3.brief: A boat powered by solar panels. It can work for long periods without refueling or frequent recharging.

S-4.brief: A sensor kit for collecting and testing water samples from a boat. It supports river surveys and water quality checks.

S-5.brief: A boat that collects algae and floating debris with AI to spot it. Helps keep waterways clean.

S-6.brief: A boat that serves as a floating base for drones, which can land on it while it moves. It extends drone reach over water.

U-1.brief: A small underwater robot connected to the surface by a cable, built on the open ArduSub software. The tether gives power and a reliable control link.

U-2.brief: A tough, lightweight fiber tether carrying power and data to an underwater vehicle.

U-3.brief: A modem that sends encrypted data through water using sound, since radio doesn't travel well underwater. Lets vehicles talk without a cable.

U-4.brief: A buoy or boat that links underwater vehicles to the surface network. It translates between sound or cable and radio.

U-5.brief: A submarine that navigates and works on its own, without a tether. It builds on the surface gateway and navigation without GPS.

U-6.brief: A fish-shaped sub that swims with body movement instead of propellers. It may be quieter and gentler on wildlife.

U-7.brief: A robot that works underwater to replant coral and remove invasive species. It supports reef and wetland recovery.

X-2.brief: A heat camera that sees warmth instead of light. It works at night and helps find people, animals and hot spots.

X-3.brief: A lightweight, open laser scanner that measures distance to build 3D shapes. Used for mapping, navigation and surveys.

X-4.brief: A compact radar that senses objects using radio waves, even in fog or darkness. It adds another way for vehicles to see their surroundings.

X-5.brief: Using several microphones to find where a sound came from by comparing arrival times. Needs shared timing, and enables sound-based detection.

X-6.brief: Turning many photos or scans into maps and 3D models, using tools like OpenDroneMap. Maps support surveys, inspections and monitoring.

X-7.brief: Combining any two or more of thermal, LiDAR and radar into one clearer picture with AI. Several sensors together beat any single sensor.

X-8.brief: Many vehicles mapping an area together and merging results into one map. Covers ground faster than one vehicle alone can.

M-1.brief: A robotic arm or claw that grabs and collects objects. It enables cleanup, repair and recovery jobs.

M-2.brief: A way to catch or recover a vehicle in flight, rather than landing it. It lets motherships bring their drones back aboard.

M-3.brief: A payload that releases items from a vehicle, like supplies or seeds. Useful for delivery, rescue and planting.

M-4.brief: A speaker payload that plays sounds or voice. It can scare animals away or let rescuers talk to people from a distance.

M-5.brief: A mechanism that drops small mesh nodes along a robot's path. It keeps a communication chain connected in places like tunnels.

M-6.brief: A launcher on shore that sends a self-inflating flotation device out to someone in the water. A fast way to get help to a swimmer.

O-1.brief: A live map showing where the OASA mesh reaches and where it is weak. It helps plan where to place new nodes.

O-2.brief: Small, solar-friendly sensor nodes that run for a long time on very little power. Basis for weather, environment and city sensing.

O-3.brief: Weather stations on the network that tell operators whether it is safe to fly or sail. A simple go or no-go answer helps prevent accidents.

O-4.brief: Tools to manage many vehicles at once: where they are, what they're doing, and who charges next. Needed to run larger fleets.

O-5.brief: Using thermal cameras and AI to detect feral hogs, and speakers to scare them away. Gives farms early warning of hog activity.

O-6.brief: A truck and trailer that carries docks, vehicles and a mesh node. A mobile base you can drive to where it is needed.

O-7.brief: A solar blimp that watches for wildfires with thermal and smoke detection. Like a fire tower in the sky that spots fires early.

O-8.brief: A mobile station that prints replacement parts and swaps them into vehicles in the field. It keeps a fleet running far from a workshop.

O-9.brief: A facility that fixes damaged devices with minimal human work. It scales up the field repair idea.

O-10.brief: Vehicles that carry broken devices to repair centers and bring parts back out. It closes the loop of a self-repairing fleet.

O-11.brief: Using thermal imagery, maps and AI to spot dry vegetation and fuel buildup near communities. It shows where fires could spread.

O-12.brief: Helping fire agencies plan and monitor controlled burns using risk maps and drops. Humans and agencies stay in charge.

O-13.brief: Planting seeds from the air and tracking how the land recovers over time using maps. It supports reforestation after fires.

O-14.brief: A network of connected sensors across a city that share data with each other and the map. The base of a living model of the city.

O-15.brief: Cameras and microphones watching for signs of someone struggling in water, like movement or screams. An early warning to alert lifeguards.

O-16.brief: A set of tools to support lifeguards: shore launcher, drone-dropped flotation and a two-way speaker. Comes in budget tiers, and supports rather than replaces lifeguards.

O-17.brief: A shore base where cleanup boats unload, recharge and relaunch on their own. It keeps ocean cleanup running continuously.

O-18.brief: Sensors on utility poles that measure air quality, weather and mosquitoes, powered by solar and linked by radio. Planned with utilities as partners.

O-19.brief: Mapping standing water where mosquitoes breed and dropping larvicide, working with county programs. It targets treatment where it counts.

O-20.brief: Patrolling land and water to spot invasive plants and animals using AI vision. Early detection makes removal easier.

O-21.brief: Helping ski patrol watch slopes, search for beacons and drop supplies. Support for trained patrollers, not a replacement.

O-22.brief: Sensor kits that anyone can host, feeding a shared open map. Connects to Meshtastic so community networks can join in.

I-1.brief: A small robot that crawls through pipes and sewers with a camera and cable or mesh link. It inspects places people can't safely go.

I-2.brief: A drone and a line-crawling robot that check power lines for damage. Reduces risky climbing and inspection by hand.

I-3.brief: Drones with cameras and LiDAR that check bridges and structures for cracks and wear. Gets close to hard-to-reach spots.

I-4.brief: A robot designed to cross steep, rocky or uneven land. Combines legged mobility with navigation that doesn't need GPS.

I-5.brief: Software that turns inspection data into clear reports and uses AI to flag defects. Makes inspections useful to the people who fix things.

I-6.brief: Drones that survey roads for potholes and wear, and flag clogged storm drains and culverts. Helps cities fix problems early.

I-7.brief: Acoustic sensors placed along water mains that listen for leaks. Catching leaks early limits water loss and repair work.

I-8.brief: Mapping the power grid ahead of time, then using robots to inspect lines and substations on their own. Builds on powerline inspection.

I-9.brief: Sensors and autonomous or assisted inspections that keep watch on dams and levees. Catching changes early helps keep communities safe.

C-1.brief: A drone that flies over a roof and checks it automatically for damage, without anyone climbing up.

C-2.brief: Regular drone mapping of a building site to track how much has been built. Shows progress against the plan.

C-3.brief: A heavy-lift drone that pressure-washes buildings and other hard-to-reach surfaces, with a physical cable link to the ground.

C-4.brief: Robots that survey a site and monitor how the build matches plans. Combines ground robots with progress tracking.

C-5.brief: A kit that checks roofs, chimneys and foundations for a home inspection. Builds on automatic roof inspection.

X-9.brief: A team of vehicles with thermal cameras that sweep an area in a planned pattern to find people. Speeds up search and rescue.

X-10.brief: A drone that drops lines or flotation devices to people stranded in floodwater. Gets help to them fast while rescuers get there.

X-11.brief: Drones that detect avalanche beacon signals to help rescue teams find buried people. Supports ski patrol and search.

X-12.brief: LiDAR maps terrain and sees through tree cover for archaeology and land survey. Reveals shapes hidden under forests.

X-13.brief: Sensors like LiDAR, a magnetometer and ground-penetrating radar, plus AI, to find buried hazards on former military sites and abandoned mines. Detection and mapping only.

SP-1.brief: A balloon that carries sensors and an OASA radio link to near space and is recovered afterward. A low-cost way to test high-altitude systems.

SP-2.brief: A small satellite carrying OASA's encrypted link and a laser comms test. The first OASA hardware in orbit.

SP-3.brief: Testing robots in places like deserts, caves and ice that resemble other planets. Teaches how to work in extreme environments.

SP-4.brief: Concept designs for vehicles that operate in thin air or low gravity, like on Mars and the Moon. Tested first in simulation.

SP-5.brief: Autonomy that keeps working when messages take a long time and no human can step in. Required for far-away missions.

MS-1.brief: A regional mesh network that keeps itself running, with private networks traveling encrypted inside it. Brings together towers, relays and nodes into shared infrastructure.

MS-2.brief: A response system where a mobile hive truck launches drones that map, search with thermal cameras, drop supplies and set up a temporary mesh. Designed for emergencies.

MS-3.brief: A farm that watches itself with sensors, scouts fields, tracks hogs and uses rovers and docks. Helps farmers see problems early.

MS-4.brief: Robots and boats that survey rivers, take samples and clean up trash on water and streets. Helps keep communities healthy.

MS-5.brief: Air, ground, surface and underwater vehicles working on a single mission. Shows that different robots can work as one team.

MS-6.brief: A solar aircraft or balloon that provides coverage and imaging from above, like a low-cost satellite. Reaches areas where ground networks don't.

MS-7.brief: The open baseline software and hardware standards that everyone can build on. A shared foundation so projects work together.

MS-8.brief: Any local chapter can build any OASA design from open plans and standard parts. Makes the community truly distributed.

MS-9.brief: High-up sensors watching for fires, like modern fire towers, plus mapping and search once a fire starts. Early warning helps firefighters.

MS-10.brief: A goal for solar aircraft that stay aloft indefinitely, using sun by day and stored energy and soaring by night. They would act as relays, cameras and sensor platforms.

MS-11.brief: A fleet that fixes itself: field cells print and swap parts, and logistics vehicles carry damaged devices to automated repair centers.

MS-12.brief: Mapping fire risk around communities, supporting controlled burns with fire agencies, and planting and tracking regrowth. Helps prevent fires and heal land.

MS-13.brief: Fleets of autonomous boats and subs clearing waterways and restoring reefs and wetlands. Cleanup and recovery at larger scale.

MS-14.brief: A living model of a city built from smart sensors that talk to each other and the world around them. Helps cities understand and respond to what is happening.

MS-15.brief: Tools that support lifeguards, never replace them: detection, shore launchers, drone drops and two-way speakers. Comes in tiers for every budget.

MS-16.brief: Robots that map collapsed buildings, caves and tunnels in 3D on their own. They go where people can't safely go.

MS-17.brief: Vehicles that aim lasers at each other in flight to share encrypted data and power. A long-term goal that builds on laser links and power beaming.

MS-18.brief: Plan a mission from one typed or spoken sentence, then steer it by voice. A long-term goal that makes a fleet easier for anyone to direct.

MS-19.brief: OASA systems tested in planetary-like environments and near space. A stepping stone toward work beyond Earth.

MS-20.brief: A self-sustaining encrypted mesh with backup comms, timing and power that keeps communities connected when other networks fail.

MS-21.brief: Roads, storm drains, water mains, the grid, dams and levees checked by autonomous systems. Helps catch problems before they become failures.

MS-22.brief: Finding buried hazards like unexploded ordnance on former U.S. military sites and abandoned mines. The same LiDAR tools can also map archaeological sites.

MS-23.brief: Anyone can host a sensor and add to a shared open map, bridged with Meshtastic. Brings everyday people into building the network.

ST-1.brief: A group of OASA CubeSats that extend the encrypted mesh into space. A long-term goal beyond the first test satellite.

ST-2.brief: Air, ground and underground robots exploring the Moon or Mars together. Takes multi-domain teamwork off Earth.

ST-3.brief: Autonomous robots that survey asteroids and moons. Far from help, they must handle problems on their own.

ST-4.brief: Off-world bases where robots build, repair and power themselves. A far-future goal for lasting presence away from Earth.

ST-5.brief: Contributing open autonomy, comms and power ideas toward probes that leave the solar system. A very long-range dream for the community.
